theme: The remaining tribal allotments, every tribe has a place
readingInstruction: Read Joshua 18:1-19:51. These chapters finish the distribution of the land. They begin with a gentle rebuke from Joshua, then describe how the remaining seven tribes receive their portions. Read for the shape of the story: the tabernacle is set up at Shiloh, and every tribe gets a place. Notice the last allotment, Joshua’s own.
settingTheScene: Israel has taken much of the land, but seven tribes have not yet received their inheritance. The tabernacle has been set up at Shiloh, and the people seem to have settled into a comfortable pause. Joshua asks a sharp question: “How long will you put off going in to take possession of the land?” The solution is a survey. Three men from each tribe are sent out to write a description of the land in seven parts, and Joshua casts lots before the LORD at Shiloh to divide it. The chapter is, in a way, about the danger of delay. God has given the land. The question is whether the people will go and take it.
observation: The whole congregation assembles at Shiloh and sets up the tent of meeting there (18:1).
“There remained among the people of Israel seven tribes whose inheritance had not yet been apportioned” (18:2).
Joshua asks, “How long will you put off going in to take possession of the land, which the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you?” (18:3).
Men are sent to survey the land and write a description in a book (18:4-9).
Joshua casts lots for them “before the LORD” (18:10).
Benjamin’s territory lies between Judah and Joseph and includes Jerusalem (called Jebus) and Gibeon (18:11-28).
Simeon’s inheritance is taken from within Judah’s allotment, “for the portion of the tribe of Judah was too large for them” (19:9).
Last of all, Joshua is given the city he asked for, Timnath-serah, “and he rebuilt the city and settled in it” (19:49-50).
interpretation:
The tone of chapter 18 is surprising. After the dramatic scenes of Jericho and Ai, the narrator pauses to describe a sluggishness. Seven tribes have not claimed their land, and Joshua asks them why. The question “How long will you put off?” hints at laziness and fear. Some of the territory remained uncleared, and it may have seemed easier to stay at Shiloh near the tabernacle than to go out and face the Canaanites.

This is a familiar spiritual pattern. After a high season of obedience, we can drift into passivity. We feel that God has done enough, and we hesitate to claim what he has given. The promise has been made, but possessing the promise requires effort. Joshua’s answer is not a rousing speech. It is a practical plan. He asks the tribes to choose surveyors, write down what they see, and bring it back. The act of describing the land makes the abstract concrete. Sometimes the first step to obedience is simply to look clearly at what God has set before us and write it down.

Then lots are cast “before the LORD” at Shiloh. The use of lots in the Old Testament expressed trust that God, not human cleverness or favoritism, determined the outcome (Proverbs 16:33). The allotments fit each tribe’s size and were set by the sovereign God. No tribe was forgotten, and none was able to claim a better deal by pulling strings. Each could say, “This is what the LORD gave me.”

The details of Benjamin’s land hold a hint of the future. It includes Jerusalem, which will be the city of David and the temple, and Gibeon, where the tabernacle will later rest. Simeon receives land inside Judah, which is a gentle fulfillment of Jacob’s prophecy in Genesis 49:7, that Simeon would be scattered in Israel.

The chapter ends with Joshua. The leader of Israel is the last to receive his portion, and he asks for a modest town in the hill country of Ephraim. He has served everyone else first. It is a quiet picture of humble leadership, and it echoes the pattern of the one who came “not to be served but to serve.” Joshua’s rebuilt city is a small sign that, in Christ, the servant is rewarded with rest.
connection: Shiloh becomes the center of Israel’s worship in Judges and 1 Samuel. The use of lots recalls Numbers 26:55 and Proverbs 16:33. Jacob’s words on Simeon are in Genesis 49:5-7. The delay in possessing the promise parallels the call in Hebrews 4:11 to “strive to enter that rest” and anticipates 2 Peter 1:5-10. Joshua’s service as the last to receive anticipates Mark 10:45.
application:
Is there an area where God has already given you something and you are still waiting at “Shiloh”? It might be a calling, a gift, a relationship, or a spiritual discipline. Ask yourself, “How long will I put off taking it?” Choose one small first step this week.

Try Joshua’s method: look at it clearly, write it down, and make a plan. If you feel a sense of calling but no action, write a one-page description of what it would look like to pursue it.

Remember also that you have been given a portion. You do not need to compare it with anyone else’s. Thank God for the specific place and work he has given you.
prayerPrompts: Confess where you have delayed or been passive in taking what God has given.
Ask him to show you what he has already given you.
Ask him for the courage to take hold of it.
